IRIS: Interpolative Rényi Iterative Self-play for Large Language Model Fine-Tuning

Wenjie Liao ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Graduate School of Information, Production and Systems, Waseda University, Fukuoka, Japan Email: jie3040@aoni    Like Wu Affiliation: Graduate School of Information, Production and Systems, Waseda University, Fukuoka, Japan Email: wulike@fuji.waseda.jp    Liangjie Zhao Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: zhaoliangjie55@gmail.com    Shihui Xu Affiliation: Graduate School of Information, Production and Systems, Waseda University, Fukuoka, Japan Email: shxu@toki.waseda.jp    Shigeru Fujimura Affiliation: Graduate School of Information, Production and Systems, Waseda University, Fukuoka, Japan Email: fujimura@waseda.jp
Abstract

Self-play fine-tuning enables large language models to improve beyond supervised fine-tuning without additional human annotations by contrasting annotated responses with self-generated ones. Many existing methods rely on a fixed divergence regime. SPIN is closely related to a KL-based regime, SPACE to a Jensen-Shannon-style objective via noise contrastive estimation, and SPIF to χ2\chi^{2}-regularized self-play. Since these divergences exhibit different strengths depending on the distributional gap between model and target, no single choice appears to provide favorable learning dynamics across training stages. We propose IRIS (Interpolative Rényi Iterative Self-play), a Rényi-based self-play fine-tuning framework with a continuously adjustable objective. IRIS decomposes into two independent tilted risk terms over annotated and synthetic data, with exponential importance weights controlled by the order parameter α\alpha. We show that several self-play objectives can be interpreted as limiting or representative regimes at particular values of α\alpha, providing a unified theoretical perspective on these methods. An adaptive order schedule further adjusts α\alpha to the distributional gap, shifting from sharper importance weighting early in training to smoother refinement near convergence. Theoretically, we establish the fixed-point property of IRIS and analyze how α\alpha controls gradient concentration. Experiments on Zephyr-7B and Qwen2.5-3B across ten benchmarks show that IRIS improves upon baselines, reaching 44.57% average score with gains across iterations. In our setting, IRIS with only 26kk annotated samples surpasses standard supervised fine-tuning trained on the full 200kk dataset.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities through post-training alignment with human preferencesMishra et al. (2022); Thoppilan et al. (2022); Chung et al. (2024); Roziere et al. (2023); Ouyang et al. (2022); OpenAI (2023); Anthropic (2024); Google (2025). The prevailing approaches, including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)Christiano et al. (2017); Azar et al. (2024); Xiong et al. (2023); Bai et al. (2022) and direct preference optimization (DPO)Rafailov et al. (2023); Tu et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2024a), rely on curated preference datasets that are expensive to acquire and difficult to scaleDong et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2023); Lee et al. (2024); Yuan et al. (2024b). This practical constraint motivates a natural question: can an LLM continue to improve beyond the ceiling of supervised fine-tuning (SFT)Ouyang et al. (2022); Tunstall et al. (2023) without any additional human-annotated data? Self-play fine-tuning (SPIN)Chen et al. (2024) provides an affirmative answer. Drawing inspiration from the self-play mechanism in AlphaGo ZeroSilver et al. (2017), SPIN frames fine-tuning as a two-player game in which the current model learns to distinguish human-written responses from those generated by its previous iteration. Empirically, SPIN enables a weak SFT model to match models trained with DPO without acquiring new human annotations, and has been applied to various LLM fieldsYuan et al. (2024a); Wu et al. (2024a); Gao et al. (2024).

Despite this conceptual elegance, SPIN exhibits several practical limitations that have motivated a growing body of follow-up workLiao et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2025b); Wang et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Yin et al. (2024); Ji et al. (2024); Ding et al. (2024); Ye et al. (2024). The gap-based objective, which contrasts real and synthetic responses through their reward difference, degenerates to a trivial constant as the two distributions converge during training. This gradient vanishing phenomenon causes instability and performance degradation in later iterations. SPACEWang et al. (2025b) addresses this problem by reformulating the objective via noise contrastive estimation (NCE)Gutmann and Hyvärinen (2010); Gutmann and Hyvärinen (2012), replacing the gap-based loss with independent classification losses for real and synthetic samples. From a complementary perspective, SGALMWu et al. (2026) constructs a GAN-style adversarial gameGoodfellow et al. (2014) within a single LLM, arriving at a structurally similar binary classification framework. Meanwhile, T-SPINWang et al. (2026) tackles the vanishing reward advantage across iterations by introducing triplets that incorporate historical model outputs alongside current ones, maintaining a persistent learning signal through the entire training process. DRIFTLiao et al. (2026) observes that SPIN applies uniform training pressure across all tokens, including those the model already predicts correctly, and proposes difference-aware masking to concentrate the gradient on error regions. Most recently, SPIFLi et al. (2026) reveals that SPIN’s implicit reward function can grow unboundedly, and introduces χ2\chi^{2} divergencePearson (1900); Neyman (1949) regularization to constrain reward magnitudes.

Each of these methods remedies a specific failure mode, but we observe that they share a common root cause. Many recent self-play fine-tuning methodsChen et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025b); Wang et al. (2026); Liao et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Alami et al. (2024); Wu et al. (2024b); Tang et al. (2025); Yuan et al. (2024c) can be interpreted through the lens of ff-divergence optimization, although they differ in data construction, optimization parameterization, and auxiliary design. The existing strategies fall into three categories accordingly. The first retains the gap-based contrastive structure under the KL divergence, strengthening it via historical anchoring, token-level masking, or opponent regularizationChen et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2026); Liao et al. (2026); Alami et al. (2024). The second replaces the gap with independent binary classification of real and synthetic samples under the Jensen-Shannon divergence, encompassing noise contrastive estimation, adversarial, and self-rewarding approachesWang et al. (2025b); Wu et al. (2026); Yuan et al. (2024c). The third enforces explicit divergence constraints or game-theoretic equilibrium formulations grounded in χ2\chi^{2} regularization or Nash convergenceLi et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2024b); Tang et al. (2025). This taxonomy suggests a practical limitation of existing methods: a single fixed divergence may not provide equally favorable learning dynamics across all stages of training. The KL divergence provides smooth gradients when the model is far from the target but loses sensitivity as the distributions converge. The χ2\chi^{2} divergence offers bounded rewards and fine-grained discrimination near convergence, yet over-penalizes outliers early on. The JS divergence ensures stability through independent optimization but is less sensitive to differences in later stages. This explains why each category excels in certain regimes while poorly in others. The comparisons are shown in Figure 1.

Building on this insight, we propose IRIS (Interpolative Rényi Iterative Self-play), a unified framework that resolves the divergence selection problem through the Rényi divergenceRényi (1961). The Rényi divergence Dα(p∥q)D_{\alpha}(p\|q) is a one-parameter generalization that continuously interpolates among the KL divergence (α→1\alpha\to 1), the χ2\chi^{2} divergence (α=2\alpha=2), and the Hellinger distance (α=1/2\alpha=1/2) van Erven and Harremoës (2014); Cichocki and Amari (2010), covering several divergence regimes closely related to those underlying existing self-play objectives. Exploiting the variational representation of this family Li and Turner (2016); Birrell et al. (2022), we derive the IRIS objective as a loss that decomposes into two independent terms over real and synthetic data, inheriting the stability of independent classification. The gradient features exponential importance weights w~∝exp⁡((α−1)⋅r)\tilde{w}\propto\exp((\alpha\!-\!1)\cdot r) that continuously concentrate learning on informative samples through a principled, tunable mechanism. We further introduce an adaptive order schedule αt\alpha_{t} that adjusts the divergence geometry to the distributional gap: larger α\alpha encourages mode-covering exploration early in training, while smaller α\alpha enables mode-seeking refinement near convergence, selecting the optimal divergence at every stage.

Theoretically, we establish the fixed-point property of IRIS, analyze its gradient structure, and show that several self-play objectives can be interpreted as representative or limiting regimes under particular choices of α\alpha. We further introduce an adaptive schedule to adjust the divergence geometry during training. Empirically, experiments on Zephyr-7BTunstall et al. (2023) and Qwen2.5-3B-InstructYang et al. (2025) across ten tasks from the Open LLM LeaderboardBeeching et al. (2023) show that IRIS reaches 44.57% average score at Iter 4, with up to 10.75-point gains over SFT on tasks such as IFEvalZhou et al. (2023). IRIS maintains stable improvements across all four iterations, whereas several strong baselines plateau or show less stable behavior later.

Our contributions. (i) We present a Rényi-based perspective that connects representative self-play objectives through distinct divergence regimes; (ii) We propose IRIS, a self-play fine-tuning framework with a continuously adjustable objective and an adaptive order schedule; (iii) We analyze the fixed-point and gradient properties of IRIS; (iv) Experiments across ten benchmarks show that IRIS outperforms other self-play baselines, while maintaining stable gains across iterations.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the necessary background on supervised fine-tuning and self-play fine-tuning, and examine existing improvements through the unifying lens of ff-divergence theory.

Supervised Fine-Tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a straightforward yet powerful approach for large language models to achieve effective task adaptation using labeled dataDong et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2023); Tan et al. (2024). Given a prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} sampled from a task-specific distribution q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) and a corresponding high-quality response 𝐲\mathbf{y} from the target distribution pdata(⋅|𝐱)p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns a policy pθp_{\theta} by maximizing the log-likelihood of annotated data:

ℒSFT(θ)=𝔼𝐱∼q(⋅),𝐲∼pdata(⋅|𝐱)[logpθ(𝐲|𝐱)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot),\,\mathbf{y}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\big]. (1)

Maximizing (1) is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence KL(pdata(⋅|𝐱)∥pθ(⋅|𝐱))\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})\right). By the non-negativity of the KL divergence, the optimal solution satisfies pθ∗(⋅|𝐱)=pdata(⋅|𝐱)p_{\theta^{*}}\!(\cdot|\mathbf{x})=p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}). However, approaching this optimum requires extensive annotated data, limiting practical applicability of SFT.

Self-Play Fine-Tuning. Self-play fine-tuningChen et al. (2024); Gao et al. (2024); Ren et al. (2024) addresses the data scarcity limitation of SFT by augmenting training with model-generated responses. The framework consists of a main player and an opponent player, both instantiated from the same LLM with different parameters. At each iteration t+1t+1, the opponent player pθtp_{\theta_{t}} generates a synthetic response 𝐲′∼pθt(⋅|𝐱)\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim p_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) for each prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The main player then updates its parameters to distinguish the annotated response 𝐲\mathbf{y} from the synthetic one 𝐲′\mathbf{y}^{\prime}. Defining the log-ratio reward and objectives as

r⁡(𝐱,𝐲^)=log⁡pθ​(𝐲^|𝐱)−log⁡pθt​(𝐲^|𝐱),r(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{y}})=\log p_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x})-\log p_{\theta_{t}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}), (2)
ℒSPIN​(θ)=𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(r⁡(𝐱,𝐲)−r⁡(𝐱,𝐲′))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPIN}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\ell\!\left(r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})-r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})\right)\right]. (3)

where ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) is a monotonically decreasing convex function, typically chosen as the logistic loss ℓ⁡(t)=log⁡(1+e−t)\ell(t)=\log(1+e^{-t}), and the expectation is taken over 𝐱∼q⁡(⋅)\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot), 𝐲∼pdata(⋅|𝐱)\mathbf{y}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}), and 𝐲′∼pθt(⋅|𝐱)\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim p_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}). The global optimum of (3) is attained when pθ=pdatap_{\theta}=p_{\mathrm{data}}, at which point the reward gap vanishes for all prompt-response pairs and the objective degenerates into a constant independent of θ\theta. This fixed-point property guarantees convergence in principle, but it also implies that the training signal weakens as pθtp_{\theta_{t}} approaches pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}, causing optimization instability in later iterations.

Self-Play Improvements as ff-Divergence Minimization. The instability described above has motivated a growing body of improvements to the self-play framework Wang et al. (2025b); Wang et al. (2026); Liao et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026); Alami et al. (2024); Wu et al. (2024b); Tang et al. (2025).A closer examination reveals that these methods, despite their diverse motivations, share a common mathematical structure rooted in ff-divergence theory Ali and Silvey (1966); Csiszár (1967). Recall that an ff-divergence Df(p∥q)=𝔼q[f(p/q)]D_{f}(p\|q)=\mathbb{E}_{q}[f(p/q)] is uniquely determined by its convex generator ff, and admits a variational representation via the Fenchel conjugate Nguyen et al. (2010) that enables tractable optimization through neural network parameterization Nowozin et al. (2016). Through this lens, existing self-play methods cluster into three families according to the divergence they implicitly minimize. The first family operates under the KL divergence, preserving the gap-based contrastive structure of SPIN while strengthening it through historical anchoring Wang et al. (2026), token-level masking Liao et al. (2026), or opponent regularization Alami et al. (2024). The second family corresponds to the Jensen-Shannon divergence Goodfellow et al. (2014), replacing the reward gap with independent binary classification of real and synthetic samples via noise contrastive estimation Wang et al. (2025b) or adversarial training Wu et al. (2026). The third family employs the χ2\chi^{2} divergence, enforcing explicit divergence constraints Li et al. (2026) or game-theoretic equilibrium formulations Wu et al. (2024b); Tang et al. (2025) that bound the reward magnitude.

This classification exposes a fundamental limitation shared by all existing approaches: each operates under a single fixed divergence throughout training. As discussed in Section 1, no single ff-divergence provides uniformly optimal learning dynamics across all stages, since different divergences exhibit complementary strengths depending on the distributional gap between the model and the target. This observation motivates a framework capable of adapting its divergence behavior during training, which we develop in the next section using the Rényi divergence familyRényi (1961); van Erven and Harremoës (2014); Li and Turner (2016); Birrell et al. (2022); Cichocki and Amari (2010); Mironov (2017); Amari (2016); Gil et al. (2013); Wang et al. (2024a).

3 Method

In this section, we present IRIS, a unified self-play fine-tuning framework built on the Rényi divergence. We construct the IRIS objective, analyze its gradient structure, and introduce an adaptive order schedule throughout training. Additional proofs and derivatives are provided in Appendix B.

3.1 The IRIS Objective

The analysis in Section II reveals that each existing self-play method commits to a single ff-divergence throughout training, and no fixed divergence provides uniformly optimal learning dynamics across all stages. To address this limitation, we seek a parameterized objective that continuously interpolates among different divergence behaviors while preserving the desirable properties of self-play fine-tuning: a fixed point at pθ=pdatap_{\theta}=p_{\mathrm{data}}, independent optimization over real and synthetic data, and tractable gradient computation. Our method builds on the tilted risk principle Li et al. (2021). For a random variable ZZ under distribution pp, the tilted risk of order s≠0s\neq 0 is defined as

ℛs​(Z,p)=1s​log⁡𝔼p​[es​Z].\mathcal{R}_{s}(Z;\,p)=\frac{1}{s}\log\mathbb{E}_{p}\!\left[e^{sZ}\right]. (4)

This quantity is the scaled cumulant generating function of ZZ, interpolating between the expectation (s→0s\to 0) and the essential supremum (s→+∞s\to+\infty). The tilted risk is connected to the Rényi divergence: for any distributions pp and qq, the Rényi divergence of order α\alpha satisfies Dα(p∥q)=ℛα(logpq;q)D_{\alpha}(p\|q)=\mathcal{R}_{\alpha}\!\left(\log\frac{p}{q};\,q\right) van Erven and Harremoës (2014), establishing the tilted risk as a building block for Rényi-based objectives. Using the log-ratio reward r⁡(𝐱,𝐲^)=log⁡pθ​(𝐲^|𝐱)−log⁡pθt​(𝐲^|𝐱)r(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{y}})=\log p_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x})-\log p_{\theta_{t}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}) defined in (2), we construct the IRIS objective for the main player by applying tilted risks of complementary orders to the real and synthetic data:

ℒIRIS​(θ,α)=−1α−1​log⁡𝔼𝐲∼pdata​[e(α−1)​r​(𝐱,𝐲)]⏟tilted reward on real data+1α​log⁡𝔼𝐲′∼pθt​[eα​r​(𝐱,𝐲′)]⏟tilted penalty on synthetic data,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta;\,\alpha)=\underbrace{-\frac{1}{\alpha\!-\!1}\,\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[e^{(\alpha-1)\,r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}\right]}_{\text{tilted reward on real data}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{\alpha}\,\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[e^{\alpha\,r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})}\right]}_{\text{tilted penalty on synthetic data}}, (5)

where the outer expectation over prompts 𝐱∼q⁡(⋅)\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot) is omitted for notational clarity, and α>0\alpha>0 with α≠1\alpha\neq 1 is the Rényi order parameter. The first term is the negated tilted risk of order (α−1)(\alpha\!-\!1) evaluated on real data, which encourages the model to assign high reward to human-annotated responses with sensitivity controlled by α\alpha. The second term is the tilted risk of order α\alpha on synthetic data, which penalizes high reward assigned to model-generated responses. The two terms operate independently on real and synthetic samples, inheriting the structural stability of independent classification Wang et al. (2025b); Wu et al. (2026). The asymmetry in orders (α−1)(\alpha\!-\!1) and α\alpha arises naturally from the Rényi variational principle Birrell et al. (2022) and ensures that the two terms remain balanced across the full range of α\alpha. A requirement for any self-play objective is that the target distribution pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} constitutes a fixed point. We establish this for IRIS.

Proposition 1 (Fixed Point).

For any α>0\alpha>0 with α≠1\alpha\neq 1, the global minimum of ℒIRIS​(θ,α)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta;\,\alpha) over θ\theta is attained at pθ=pdatap_{\theta}=p_{\mathrm{data}}. At this optimum,

ℒIRIS(θ∗;α)=−1αDα(pdata∥pθt),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta^{*};\,\alpha)=-\frac{1}{\alpha}\,D_{\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\|p_{\theta_{t}}), (6)

where DαD_{\alpha} denotes the Rényi divergence of order α\alpha. Furthermore, if pθt=pdatap_{\theta_{t}}=p_{\mathrm{data}}, then ℒIRIS​(θ∗,α)=0\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta^{*};\,\alpha)=0, confirming that the equilibrium pθ=pθt=pdatap_{\theta}=p_{\theta_{t}}=p_{\mathrm{data}} is a fixed point of the iterative self-play process.

Gradient Analysis and Importance Weighting. To understand the optimization dynamics of IRIS, we derive the gradient of (5) with respect to θ\theta and analyze how order α\alpha controls the model training.

Proposition 2 (Gradient Structure).

The gradient of ℒIRIS​(θ,α)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta;\,\alpha) with respect to θ\theta takes the form

∇θℒIRIS=−𝔼𝐲∼pdata​[w~+​(𝐲)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(𝐲|𝐱)]+𝔼𝐲′∼pθt​[w~−​(𝐲′)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(𝐲′|𝐱)],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[\tilde{w}^{+}\!(\mathbf{y})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[\tilde{w}^{-}\!(\mathbf{y}^{\prime})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})\right], (7)

where the normalized importance weights are

w~+​(𝐲)=e(α−1)​r​(𝐱,𝐲)𝔼pdata​[e(α−1)​r],w~−​(𝐲′)=eα​r​(𝐱,𝐲′)𝔼pθt​[eα​r].\tilde{w}^{+}\!(\mathbf{y})=\frac{e^{(\alpha-1)\,r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}}{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[e^{(\alpha-1)\,r}\right]},\qquad\tilde{w}^{-}\!(\mathbf{y}^{\prime})=\frac{e^{\alpha\,r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})}}{\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[e^{\alpha\,r}\right]}. (8)

The gradient in (7) admits a natural interpretation as importance-weighted likelihood updates: real responses are reinforced while synthetic ones are suppressed, with exponential weights acting as a differentiable attention mechanism over samples. For α>1\alpha>1, w~+∝exp⁡((α−1)​r)\tilde{w}^{+}\propto\exp((\alpha\!-\!1)r) emphasizes real responses that already receive high reward, whereas w~−∝exp⁡(α​r)\tilde{w}^{-}\propto\exp(\alpha r) concentrates on synthetic responses the model incorrectly favors, steering updates toward the most informative samples on both sides. The order α\alpha thereby governs the sharpness of reweighting, smoothly interpolating between uniform gradients at α→1\alpha\to 1 and highly concentrated ones at large α\alpha, and yields a continuously adjustable soft counterpart to hard selection schemes. This exponential tilting further connects IRIS to tilted empirical risk minimization Li et al. (2021), where α\alpha balances average-case and worst-case performance.

Unification of Existing Methods. A notable consequence of the tilted risk construction is that the IRIS objective recovers the divergence families underlying existing self-play methods at specific values of α\alpha, confirming that these methods were implicitly operating within the Rényi family. The independent treatment of real and synthetic terms in (5) further parallels the decoupled structure of SPACE Wang et al. (2025b) and SGALM Wu et al. (2026) under the Jensen-Shannon divergence. The correspondences of various regimes are summarized in Table 1 and three informative regimes are listed below:

  • •

    KL regime (α→1\alpha\to 1). Using the limit 1s​log⁡𝔼⁡[es​Z]→𝔼⁡[Z]\frac{1}{s}\log\mathbb{E}[e^{sZ}]\to\mathbb{E}[Z] as s→0s\to 0, ℒIRIS\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}} converges to −𝔼pdata​[r]+log⁡𝔼pθt​[er]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}[r]+\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}[e^{r}], the Donsker-Varadhan form of the KL divergence Donsker and Varadhan (1983), and the importance weights become uniform. This recovers the divergence regime of SPIN Chen et al. (2024) together with its gap-based variants Wang et al. (2026); Liao et al. (2026); Alami et al. (2024), which approximate this KL objective via logistic losses.

  • •

    χ2\chi^{2} regime (α=2\alpha=2). The identity 𝔼pθt[e2​r]=1+χ2(pθ∥pθt)\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}[e^{2r}]=1+\chi^{2}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\theta_{t}}) implies that the second term directly penalizes the χ2\chi^{2} divergence between the model and the opponent, which aligns with the bounded-reward formulations of SPIF Li et al. (2026), SPPO Wu et al. (2024b), and RSPO Tang et al. (2025).

  • •

    Hellinger regime (α=1/2\alpha=1/2). Under the squared Hellinger distance, w~+∝e−r/2\tilde{w}^{+}\!\propto e^{-r/2} emphasizes underperforming real responses, producing mode-covering behavior absent from prior methods.

3.2 Adaptive Order Schedule

The unification established above motivates a natural question: rather than committing to a single α\alpha throughout training, can we adapt αt\alpha_{t} at each iteration? This question is central to IRIS, because the appropriate divergence geometry depends on the current distributional gap between the policy and the target. We therefore consider two complementary strategies for choosing the order during training.

Distributional Gap Feedback. We set αt\alpha_{t} based on the estimated divergence between the model and target distributions:

αt=1+c⋅D^t,D^t=𝔼𝐲∼pdata​[rt​(𝐱,𝐲)]−𝔼𝐲′∼pθt​[rt​(𝐱,𝐲′)],\alpha_{t}=1+c\cdot\hat{D}_{t},\qquad\hat{D}_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[r_{t}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[r_{t}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})\right], (9)

where c>0c>0 is a scaling constant and D^t\hat{D}_{t} is the expected reward gap at the beginning of iteration tt, serving as a proxy for the distributional distanceChen et al. (2024). This choice ties the schedule directly to the training signal already used by self-play, and therefore avoids introducing an additional external criterion for tuning αt\alpha_{t}. When the model is far from the target (D^t\hat{D}_{t} large), αt\alpha_{t} is large, promoting mode-covering exploration through the χ2\chi^{2}-like behavior and concentrated importance weights. This places more emphasis on informative high-gap samples, which is beneficial when the model and data distributions remain substantially separated. As the model converges (D^t→0\hat{D}_{t}\to 0), αt\alpha_{t} decreases toward 11, transitioning to the KL regime that provides smoother, more uniform gradients near equilibrium.

Geometric Annealing. For simplicity and reproducibility, we also consider a predetermined schedule:

αt=αmax⋅(αminαmax)t/T,\alpha_{t}=\alpha_{\max}\cdot\left(\frac{\alpha_{\min}}{\alpha_{\max}}\right)^{t/T}, (10)

which interpolates from αmax\alpha_{\max} to αmin\alpha_{\min} over TT iterations. This schedule requires no statistics and is straightforward to implement. Both strategies share the same inductive bias: larger α\alpha early for exploration through importance weights, and smaller α\alpha later for refinement through uniform gradients. In Section IV, we compare both strategies and find that distributional gap feedback outperforms geometric annealing, as it responds to dynamics rather than following a predetermined trajectory.

3.3 Algorithm Summary

We summarize IRIS in Algorithm 1. The procedure follows the standard self-play pipeline Chen et al. (2024), with two modifications: (i) the loss function in (5) replaces the gap-based or fixed-divergence objectives of prior methods, and (ii) the order αt\alpha_{t} is updated at each iteration based on reward statistics. In practice, the log-sum-exp operations in (5) are stabilized by subtracting the batch maximum before exponentiation Blanchard et al. (2021), the importance weights w~±\tilde{w}^{\pm} in (8) are normalized within each mini-batch to prevent any single sample from dominating the gradient, and the reward gap D^t\hat{D}_{t} in (9) is estimated from the first mini-batch of each iteration at negligible additional cost. IRIS is fully compatible with existing self-play codebases Chen et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025b), requiring only a substitution of the loss computation module while leaving the generation, data processing, and distributed training components unchanged.

4 Experiments

In this section, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of IRIS. We first describe the experimental settings, and then report the main results with analyses. Finally, we present ablation studies on the adaptive order schedule. More details are provided in Appendix C.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models and training. Following SPIN Chen et al. (2024) and subsequent works Wang et al. (2025b); Wang et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026), we randomly sample 50kk prompt-response pairs from the first round of interactions in Ultrachat200k Ding et al. (2023) and evaluate on Zephyr-7B-SFT-Full Tunstall et al. (2023) and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct Yang et al. (2025). At each of five self-play iterations (Iter 0 through Iter 4), we generate one synthetic response per prompt and combine it with the annotated response for training. We use RMSProp Hinton et al. (2012) as optimizer with a global batch size of 64 and 2 epochs per iteration. For the adaptive schedule in (9), we set c=0.5c=0.5 with αt∈[0.5,3.0]\alpha_{t}\in[0.5,3.0]. All the experiments run on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs using the Alignment Handbook Tunstall et al. (2024) and Accelerate Gugger et al. (2022).

Evaluation and baselines. We evaluate on ten diverse tasks from the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard Beeching et al. (2023), grouped into mathematical and logical reasoning (GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), MATH Hendrycks et al. (2021b), MUSR Sprague et al. (2024)), multi-domain knowledge (MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021a), MMLU-Pro Wang et al. (2024b), GPQA Rein et al. (2023)), commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag Zellers et al. (2019), WinoGrande Sakaguchi et al. (2021), BBH Suzgun et al. (2023)), and instruction following (IFEval Zhou et al. (2023)), using the Language Model Evaluation Harness Gao et al. (2023). We compare IRIS against SFT trained on the full 200kk dataset, SPIN Chen et al. (2024), SPACE Wang et al. (2025b), T-SPIN Wang et al. (2026), and SPIF Li et al. (2026). All self-play methods are trained on the same 50kk subset with identical generation and training configurations for fair comparison.

4.2 Main Results

Comparison across methods. Table 2 presents the main results on Zephyr-7B across all ten benchmarks. Several observations emerge from these results. First, all self-play methods surpass both the pretrained model and SFT, confirming the effectiveness of iterative self-play even with limited annotated data. Second, IRIS consistently achieves the highest average score across all iterations, reaching 44.57% at Iter 4, compared to 43.56% for T-SPIN, 42.40% for SPACE and SPIF, and 41.17% for SPIN. Third, the improvements from IRIS are particularly pronounced on MATH, MUSR and IFEval tasks with 1.82-point, 3.10-point and 10.75-point increases respectively compared with SFT base, where the adaptive divergence schedule provides the greatest benefit. Results on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, which also exhibit similar overall trends, are provided in Appendix C.3.

Comparison to training with more epochs. We examine whether the iterative gains of self-play can be matched by simply training longer on fixed synthetic responses, extending iteration 0 to five epochs and comparing against iteration 1 with two epochs on regenerated responses (Figure 2). The average score plateaus near 42.1 after five epochs, remaining well below the 43.1 that iteration 1 achieves with two epochs alone, with especially large gaps on GSM8K and IFEval. The bottleneck lies in the stagnation of negative samples: as the policy improves, the fixed synthetic responses grow increasingly uninformative. Regenerating responses at iteration 1 supplies negatives that reflect the model’s current weaknesses, and in IRIS additionally triggers a recalibration of αt\alpha_{t} via the adaptive schedule (9), keeping the objective aligned with the evolving distributional gap. These results confirm that data regeneration, not prolonged training on static data, drives cross-iteration improvement.

Training dynamics. Reward decline on high-quality responses is a known issue in preference alignment Feng et al. (2024); Pal et al. (2024); Rafailov et al. (2024); Xiao et al. (2024) and was first studied in self-play fine-tuning by SPACE Wang et al. (2025b). Figure 3 compares IRIS and SPIN at Iter 0. Panels (a) and (b) show that SPIN enlarges the reward margin, but the reward on annotated responses decreases during training, while the reward on synthetic responses decreases faster. This is a limitation of gap-based optimization: SPIN improves the objective through the relative difference r⁡(𝐱,𝐲)−r⁡(𝐱,𝐲′)r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})-r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime}), without directly increasing the absolute reward on real data. As a result, a larger margin does not necessarily mean better modeling of high-quality responses. In contrast, IRIS increases the reward on real data and decreases it on synthetic data, since its objective optimizes both terms separately via a tilted reward on annotated data and a tilted penalty on synthetic ones. The margin in IRIS reflects progress toward the target distribution. Panel (c) shows under distributional gap feedback, αt\alpha_{t} starts near 3.0 and approaches 2.0, indicating a shift from sharper reweighting early in training to smoother refinement, with training cost recorded in Appendix C.2.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Effect of the adaptive order schedule. Table 3 compares five strategies for setting the Rényi order α\alpha on Zephyr-7B. Fixing α\alpha at 0.5, 1.5, or 2.0 throughout training corresponds to the Hellinger, intermediate, and χ2\chi^{2} regimes, respectively. The results reveal a clear tradeoff between stability and aggressiveness: α=0.5\alpha=0.5 produces the most stable trajectory with no degradation across iterations but converges slowly, α=2.0\alpha=2.0 delivers the strongest initial gains but becomes unstable after Iter 2, and α=1.5\alpha=1.5 balances the two yet still plateaus at a lower final performance level. Geometric annealing from αmax=2.5\alpha_{\max}=2.5 to αmin=0.8\alpha_{\min}=0.8 surpasses all fixed choices by combining early exploration with late refinement within each iteration. The distributional gap feedback schedule in (9) consistently achieves the highest score at every iteration beyond Iter 0, as it calibrates the order to the actual divergence between the policy and the data distribution rather than following a predetermined decay.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters. We examine the sensitivity of IRIS to the scaling constant cc in (9) and the clipping bounds [αmin,αmax][\alpha_{\min},\alpha_{\max}], both evaluated at Iter 1 on Zephyr-7B. Figure 4(a) reports the average score for c∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0}c\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0\}: all four values fall between 42.71% and 43.12%, a range of less than 0.5 points, indicating that the feedback gain has minimal impact on final performance so long as it remains within a reasonable magnitude. Figure 4(b) presents a heatmap over αmax∈{1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0}\alpha_{\max}\in\{1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0\} and αmin∈{0.3,0.5,0.8,1.0}\alpha_{\min}\in\{0.3,0.5,0.8,1.0\}. Performance exceeds 42.6% whenever αmax≥2.0\alpha_{\max}\geq 2.0 and αmin≤0.8\alpha_{\min}\leq 0.8, confirming that the schedule tolerates a broad operating region, while the combination αmax=3.0\alpha_{\max}=3.0, αmin=0.5\alpha_{\min}=0.5 achieves the peak of 43.12%. Based on these results, we adopt c=0.5c=0.5, αmax=3.0\alpha_{\max}=3.0, and αmin=0.5\alpha_{\min}=0.5 as default values throughout all other experiments.

Data efficiency. Following the protocol of SPACE Wang et al. (2025b) and T-SPIN Wang et al. (2026), we compare IRIS with SFT under varying amounts of annotated data. We train IRIS on subsets of 14kk, 26kk, and 50kk samples for two iterations, and SFT on 50kk, 100kk, and 200kk samples. Figure 4(c) shows that IRIS with only 26kk annotated responses reaches 42.53% after two iterations, surpassing SFT trained on the full 200kk dataset (41.99%) by 0.54 points while using roughly one eighth of the annotated data. When the annotated set grows to 50kk, IRIS further improves to 43.12%, exceeding 200kk SFT by 1.13 points. The gap widens as more annotated data becomes available, suggesting that the adaptive schedule extracts progressively richer training signal from larger annotation pools. These results confirm that iterative self-play amplifies the value of limited annotations, and that the adaptive divergence mechanism in IRIS provides complementary gains by tailoring the Rényi order to the current policy state at each iteration rather than relying on a fixed and potentially suboptimal divergence measure.

5 Conclusion and discussion

We have presented IRIS, a self-play fine-tuning framework grounded in the Rényi divergence family. The IRIS objective decomposes into two independent tilted risk terms over annotated and synthetic data, yielding decoupled optimization and continuously adjustable importance weighting through the order parameter α\alpha. We have shown that several representative self-play objectives, including SPIN, SPACE, and SPIF, can be interpreted within the same Rényi-based perspective through particular divergence regimes. The adaptive order schedule shifts from sharper importance weighting early in training to smoother refinement near convergence, responding to the observed distributional gap rather than following a fixed trajectory. Experiments on Zephyr-7B and Qwen2.5-3B across ten benchmarks show that IRIS is competitive with and often improves upon strong baselines, while maintaining stable gains across iterations and ultimately reaching 44.57% average score at Iter 4.

Limitations and Future Work. Like all existing self-play methods, IRIS assumes a fixed target distribution throughout training. Extending the framework to non-stationary settings where the target evolves through online interaction is a natural direction, and recent advances in game-theoretic alignment via no-regret learning Zhang et al. (2025) and last-iterate convergence guarantees Wang et al. (2025a) provide promising theoretical foundations for such an extension. Our evaluation is restricted to single-turn generation on models up to 7B parameters; applying IRIS to multi-turn dialogue and scaling to larger architectures through parameter-efficient methods Hu et al. (2022) remain unexplored. On the theoretical side, the adaptive schedule in (9) is empirically effective but lacks formal regret bounds characterizing the optimal trajectory of αt\alpha_{t} on the Rényi manifold. Finally, combining the Rényi family with broader divergence classes Wang et al. (2024a) or extending the mechanism to token-level order adaptation may yield further gains.

Appendix A Additional Related Work

A.1 Rényi Divergence and Information Geometry

The Rényi divergence [60] belongs to the broader family of α\alpha-divergences studied in information geometry [3, 14], with van Erven and Harremoes̈ [72] establishing key properties including monotonicity in the order α\alpha and continuity at the KL limit. Its variational representation [9, 42] enables tractable optimization in high-dimensional settings and has been applied to variational inference through black-box α\alpha-divergence minimization [34], where the order parameter provides a smooth interpolation between mass-covering and zero-forcing inference. Beyond generative modeling, Rényi divergence underpins Rényi differential privacy [46], which yields tighter composition bounds than standard (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP through moment-based accounting, and connects to distributionally robust optimization via tilted empirical risk minimization [41], where the tilting parameter controls the tradeoff between average-case and worst-case objectives. Gil [26] and Wang et al. [73] offer comprehensive treatments of Rényi-based estimation and general divergence optimization, respectively. Our work applies the Rényi variational principle to self-play fine-tuning, where the order parameter simultaneously governs the divergence geometry and the importance weighting scheme for adaptive sample selection.

A.2 Preference Optimization for Language Models

Post-training alignment of LLMs has been extensively studied through preference-based methods. RLHF [12, 52, 6] first trains a reward model on pairwise human preferences and then optimizes the language model policy via proximal policy optimization. Direct preference optimization (DPO) [56] bypasses explicit reward modeling by reparameterizing the reward through the policy itself, and has inspired a family of variants that simplify the pipeline further, including IPO [5], SimPO [45], KTO [22], and ORPO [36]. Iterative extensions [83, 69, 80, 91] regenerate preference pairs at each round, sharing the iterative structure of self-play while still relying on a preference oracle for labeling. Self-play fine-tuning [11] operates in a distinct setting: it replaces pairwise preference judgments with the binary distinction between expert-annotated and model-generated responses, removing the need for any preference labels. IRIS inherits this label-free property while introducing adaptive divergence control that is absent from both preference-based and existing self-play approaches.

Appendix B Theoretical Proofs

In this section, we provide detailed proofs of Propositions 1 and 2 stated in Section 3, followed by rigorous derivations of the three special-case regimes listed in Table 1. Throughout, we condition on a fixed prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} and suppress the dependence on 𝐱\mathbf{x} for notational brevity; all expectations over prompts can be restored by an outer average over 𝐱∼q⁡(⋅)\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot).

=−𝔼pdata​[w~+​(𝐲)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(𝐲|𝐱)].\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[\tilde{w}^{+}\!(\mathbf{y})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\right]. (21)

B.3 Derivation of Special Cases

We rigorously derive the three limiting and boundary regimes stated in Section 3.1, confirming that each corresponds to a known divergence family.

B.3.1 KL Regime (α→1\alpha\to 1)

The tilted risk ℛs​(Z,p)=1s​log⁡𝔼p​[es​Z]\mathcal{R}_{s}(Z;p)=\frac{1}{s}\log\mathbb{E}_{p}[e^{sZ}] is the scaled cumulant generating function of ZZ. A standard Taylor expansion of the moment generating function around s=0s=0 gives

𝔼p​[es​Z]=1+s​𝔼p​[Z]+s22​𝔼p​[Z2]+O⁡(s3),\mathbb{E}_{p}\!\left[e^{sZ}\right]=1+s\,\mathbb{E}_{p}[Z]+\frac{s^{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p}[Z^{2}]+O(s^{3}), (23)

so 1s​log⁡(1+s​𝔼p​[Z]+O⁡(s2))=𝔼p​[Z]+O⁡(s)\frac{1}{s}\log(1+s\,\mathbb{E}_{p}[Z]+O(s^{2}))=\mathbb{E}_{p}[Z]+O(s), yielding lims→0ℛs​(Z,p)=𝔼p​[Z]\lim_{s\to 0}\mathcal{R}_{s}(Z;p)=\mathbb{E}_{p}[Z]. In ℒIRIS\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}, the first term has order s1=α−1→0s_{1}=\alpha\!-\!1\to 0 while the second has order s2=α→1s_{2}=\alpha\to 1. Taking these limits:

limα→1ℒIRIS​(θ,α)=−𝔼pdata​[r⁡(𝐱,𝐲)]+log⁡𝔼pθt​[er⁡(𝐱,𝐲′)].\lim_{\alpha\to 1}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta;\alpha)=-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\right]+\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[e^{r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})}\right]. (24)

This is the negated Donsker-Varadhan representation [21] of KL(pdata∥pθt)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{data}}\|p_{\theta_{t}}) evaluated at the test function f=rf=r. Since r=log⁡(pθ/pθt)r=\log(p_{\theta}/p_{\theta_{t}}) and pθp_{\theta} is a normalized distribution, the second term evaluates to log∫pθt⋅(pθ/pθt)d𝐲=log1=0\log\int p_{\theta_{t}}\cdot(p_{\theta}/p_{\theta_{t}})\,d\mathbf{y}=\log 1=0. The objective therefore reduces to −𝔼pdata​[log⁡pθ​(𝐲|𝐱)]+constant-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})]+\mathrm{constant}, recovering the negative log-likelihood used in supervised fine-tuning. This is the same KL regime as SPIN [11] and its variants [76, 43, 1], which approximate this objective through logistic losses on the reward gap r⁡(𝐱,𝐲)−r⁡(𝐱,𝐲′)r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})-r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime}).

Correspondingly, the importance weights in (8) satisfy w~+​(𝐲)=e(α−1)​r/𝔼⁡[e(α−1)​r]→1\tilde{w}^{+}\!(\mathbf{y})=e^{(\alpha-1)r}/\mathbb{E}[e^{(\alpha-1)r}]\to 1 as α→1\alpha\to 1, confirming that the gradient becomes a uniformly weighted likelihood update.

B.3.2 χ2\chi^{2} Regime (α=2\alpha=2)

Setting α=2\alpha=2 in (5) and using er=ρ=pθ/pθte^{r}=\rho=p_{\theta}/p_{\theta_{t}}:

ℒIRIS​(θ,2)=−log⁡𝔼pdata​[ρ]+12​log⁡𝔼pθt​[ρ2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta;2)=-\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[\rho\right]+\frac{1}{2}\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[\rho^{2}\right]. (25)

We analyze each term. For the second term, expanding the expectation:

𝔼pθt[ρ2]=∫pθt(𝐲)(pθ​(𝐲)pθt​(𝐲))2d𝐲=∫pθ​(𝐲)2pθt​(𝐲)d𝐲=1+χ2(pθ∥pθt),\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[\rho^{2}\right]=\int p_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y})\left(\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})}{p_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y})}\right)^{\!2}\,d\mathbf{y}=\int\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})^{2}}{p_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y})}\,d\mathbf{y}=1+\chi^{2}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\theta_{t}}), (26)

where the last equality follows from the definition χ2(p∥q)=∫(p−q)2/q=∫p2/q−1\chi^{2}(p\|q)=\int(p-q)^{2}/q=\int p^{2}/q-1 [54]. Therefore 12log𝔼pθt[ρ2]=12log(1+χ2(pθ∥pθt))\frac{1}{2}\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}[\rho^{2}]=\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\chi^{2}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\theta_{t}})), which directly penalizes the χ2\chi^{2} divergence between the current policy and the opponent, confirming the connection to the bounded-reward formulations in SPIF [40] and SPPO [81]. The importance weights at α=2\alpha=2 become w~+∝er=pθ/pθt\tilde{w}^{+}\!\propto e^{r}=p_{\theta}/p_{\theta_{t}} and w~−∝e2​r=(pθ/pθt)2\tilde{w}^{-}\!\propto e^{2r}=(p_{\theta}/p_{\theta_{t}})^{2}, concentrating quadratically on synthetic responses that the model incorrectly favors.

B.3.3 Hellinger Regime (α=1/2\alpha=1/2)

Setting α=1/2\alpha=1/2 gives orders α−1=−1/2\alpha\!-\!1=-1/2 and α=1/2\alpha=1/2 for the two tilted risks:

ℒIRIS(θ;12)=2log𝔼pdata[ρ−1/2]+2log𝔼pθt[ρ1/2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IRIS}}(\theta;\tfrac{1}{2})=2\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}}\!\left[\rho^{-1/2}\right]+2\log\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[\rho^{1/2}\right]. (27)

The second expectation evaluates to the Bhattacharyya coefficient [8]:

𝔼pθt​[ρ1/2]=∫pθt​(𝐲)​(pθ​(𝐲)pθt​(𝐲))1/2​𝑑𝐲=∫pθ​(𝐲)​pθt​(𝐲)​𝑑𝐲=1−H2​(pθ,pθt),\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta_{t}}}\!\left[\rho^{1/2}\right]=\int p_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y})\left(\frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})}{p_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y})}\right)^{\!1/2}\!\!d\mathbf{y}=\int\!\sqrt{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})\,p_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y})}\,d\mathbf{y}=1-H^{2}(p_{\theta},\,p_{\theta_{t}}), (28)

where H2​(p,q)=1−∫p​qH^{2}(p,q)=1-\int\sqrt{pq} denotes the squared Hellinger distance [72]. The importance weights at α=1/2\alpha=1/2 are w~+∝e−r/2=(pθt/pθ)1/2\tilde{w}^{+}\!\propto e^{-r/2}=(p_{\theta_{t}}/p_{\theta})^{1/2}, which assign larger weight to annotated responses where the current model underperforms relative to the opponent, and w~−∝er/2=(pθ/pθt)1/2\tilde{w}^{-}\!\propto e^{r/2}=(p_{\theta}/p_{\theta_{t}})^{1/2}, which mildly penalizes synthetic responses where the model overestimates. This inverse-exponential weighting induces a mode-covering effect that ensures the model does not ignore low-probability but high-quality real responses, a behavior absent from the KL and χ2\chi^{2} regimes where w~+\tilde{w}^{+} increases with rr.

Appendix C More Experimental Details

In this section, we provide implementation details, computational cost analysis, and full experimental results on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct[84] that complement the main experiments in Section 4.

C.1 Implementation Details

We build our codebase on the Alignment Handbook[70] and use the Accelerate library[29] for distributed training across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with 80GB memory each. Following Chen et al.[11] and Wang et al.[76], we employ RMSProp[35] with no weight decay as the optimizer and set the maximum sequence length to 2048 tokens. The warmup ratio is 10% of the total training steps, followed by a cosine learning rate schedule with a peak learning rate of 5×10−75\times 10^{-7}. We use a per-GPU batch size of 8, yielding a global batch size of 64. All training is conducted in bfloat16 mixed precision with DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3[57] and FlashAttention-2[17] for memory efficiency. For synthetic response generation, we use the Accelerate library in distributed mode with a global batch size of 256. At each iteration, we generate one response per prompt using nucleus sampling with temperature 0.70.7 and top​-​p=0.9\mathrm{top\text{-}}p=0.9, with a maximum generation length of 2048 tokens. Following SPIN[11] and SPACE[75], we sample 50kk prompt-response pairs exclusively from the first round of interactions in UltraChat200k[19]. The prompts are formatted using the ChatML template consistent with each base model’s instruction-tuning format.

C.2 Computational Costs

Table 4 reports the wall-clock time for generation and training at each iteration on both Zephyr-7B and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, together with the adaptive order αt\alpha_{t} selected by the distributional gap feedback schedule in Eq. (9). Generation costs remain constant across iterations at 0.81 hours for Zephyr-7B and 0.35 hours for Qwen2.5-3B, as the same number of synthetic responses (50kk) are produced each time using the Accelerate library[29] with distributed inference across 8 H100 GPUs.

Training time exhibits a mild but consistent decrease over iterations, dropping from 3.31 to 3.17 hours on Zephyr-7B and from 1.45 to 1.35 hours on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. This trend directly reflects the decay of αt\alpha_{t} across iterations. In early iterations, larger α\alpha produces sharper exponential importance weights w~±∝exp⁡((α−1)​r)\tilde{w}^{\pm}\propto\exp((\alpha\!-\!1)\,r) in Eq. (8), which increases the computational overhead of log-sum-exp stabilization and per-batch weight normalization. As training progresses and αt\alpha_{t} decreases, the tilted risk terms in Eq. (5) reduce toward simpler expectations with near-uniform weights, lowering this overhead. The total cost for five iterations is 20.2 hours for Zephyr-7B, and 8.7 hours for Qwen2.5-3B.

C.3 Experimental Results on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct

Table 5 presents the performance of all methods on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct across ten benchmarks over five self-play iterations. The overall trends are consistent with the Zephyr-7B results in Table 2. IRIS achieves the highest average score of 56.18% at Iter 4, surpassing T-SPIN (55.73%), SPACE (54.52%), SPIF (54.21%), and SPIN (53.88%) by margins of 0.45, 1.66, 1.97, and 2.30 points, respectively. IRIS maintains monotonic improvement across all five iterations, whereas SPIN peaks at Iter 2 before declining, and SPIF similarly degrades after Iter 2. The gains are most pronounced on IFEval, where IRIS obtains a 19.74-point improvement over the base model, and on MMLU, where IRIS reaches 68.93% compared to 66.64% for SPIN. With only 50kk annotated samples trained for four iterations, IRIS surpasses SFT trained on the full 200kk dataset by 3.99 points, confirming that the adaptive divergence mechanism provides consistent benefits across model scales. Figure 5 provides a visual comparison on GSM8K, IFEval, and average score across iterations.
